title: Complex Exponential
body:
Euler's formula is the hinge of the whole course:

$$
e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta
$$

so a point on the unit circle, a rotation, and an exponential are the same object written three
ways. [[Polar Form]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] already said $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$; this
says that bracket is $e^{i\theta}$, and everything gets shorter.

## The complex Fourier series

The trigonometric series has two families of coefficients and two orthogonality identities to
juggle. Rearranging Euler's formula gives

$$
\cos(nx) = \frac{e^{inx} + e^{-inx}}{2}, \qquad \sin(nx) = \frac{e^{inx} - e^{-inx}}{2i}
$$

and substituting collapses the whole thing into one sum over **all** integers, positive and
negative:

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n e^{inx}, \qquad
c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)e^{-inx}\,dx
$$

One family of [[Fourier Coefficients]] instead of two, one integral instead of two, and the
relationship back is $c_n = \frac{a_n - ib_n}{2}$ for $n > 0$, with $c_{-n} = \overline{c_n}$ when
$f$ is real. **The negative frequencies are not physical**; they are the bookkeeping that lets a
real cosine be written as two counter-rotating complex phasors.

## Why it is worth the imaginary numbers

- Differentiation becomes multiplication: $\frac{d}{dx}e^{inx} = in\,e^{inx}$. This is the
  derivative property that makes the [[Fourier Transform]] turn a differential equation into an
  algebraic one, and it is why [[Differential Equations]] and Fourier analysis keep meeting.
- Multiplying two exponentials adds their exponents, so phase shifts are addition. The
  trigonometric identities you would otherwise memorise are just $e^{a}e^{b} = e^{a+b}$.
- Sampling $e^{2\pi i k/N}$ at $N$ evenly spaced angles gives the [[Roots of Unity]], which are the
  entries of the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] matrix.
- $|e^{i\theta}| = 1$ always, so the magnitude of $c_n$ is the amplitude of that frequency and its
  argument is the phase. **Amplitude and phase come out of one complex number** instead of being
  reconstructed from an $a_n$ and $b_n$ pair.

See [[Complex Numbers]] (MATH 1203) for the arithmetic and the geometry, and [[Complex Integration]]
for what happens when you let $\theta$ trace a path rather than a circle.
